title: Redis Data Types: A Working Handbook
summary: A dense, practical tour of Redis's core data types — strings, lists, sets, sorted sets, and hashes — covering their internal encodings, the commands that make each one worth reaching for, Big-O costs, and the mistakes that turn a fast cache into a stalled server.

chapters.title: Redis Foundations: Keys, Values, and the Single Thread
points: Redis is an in-memory key-value store: keys are always binary-safe strings, values are one of the typed structures (string, list, set, sorted set, hash, plus stream/bitmap/HLL)
Everything hangs off a flat keyspace — there are no tables or nested documents; structure lives in the key name (e.g. `user:1000:sessions`) and in the value type
Command execution is single-threaded: every command runs to completion atomically, so no locks or transactions are needed for a single command
Consequence of single-threading: one O(N) command over a million elements blocks every other client for the whole duration — latency is a shared resource
`TYPE key` returns the type of a value; commands are type-checked and return `WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value` on mismatch
Key naming convention: colon-delimited namespaces `object-type:id:field`, e.g. `user:1000:profile`, `cart:42:items` — Redis does not enforce it but tooling and `SCAN` patterns depend on it
TTL is a property of the key, not the value: `EXPIRE key 60`, `TTL key` (returns -1 no TTL, -2 no key), `PERSIST key` removes it
Gotcha: most write commands that replace a value (`SET`) clear the TTL, while commands that mutate in place (`APPEND`, `LPUSH`, `HSET`, `INCR`) keep it — `SET key v KEEPTTL` preserves it
`DEL key` is O(N) in the number of elements freed; `UNLINK key` reclaims memory in a background thread and returns immediately — prefer `UNLINK` for large collections
`EXISTS`, `RENAME`, `COPY`, `RANDOMKEY` work across all types; `KEYS pattern` is O(N) over the whole keyspace and must never run in production — use `SCAN` with a cursor
`SCAN cursor MATCH pattern COUNT n` gives a bounded-work, cursor-based iteration: guarantees elements present the whole time are returned at least once, may return duplicates
Every type has a small-size compact encoding and a large-size general encoding; `OBJECT ENCODING key` reveals which one is in play and is the main memory debugging tool
Choosing a type is a choice about access pattern: 'do I read the whole value or one field?', 'do I need order?', 'do I need uniqueness?', 'do I need ranking?'
Redis is not schemaless-free: because you cannot query by value, the access pattern must be designed into the key structure before you write the first command

chapters.title: Strings: The Byte Array That Does Everything
points: A Redis string is a binary-safe byte array up to 512 MB — it can hold text, JSON, a serialized protobuf, a JPEG, or a counter
`SET key value` / `GET key` are both O(1); `SET` overwrites regardless of existing type
`SET` option flags: `EX seconds`, `PX milliseconds`, `EXAT unix-time`, `NX` (only if absent), `XX` (only if present), `GET` (return old value), `KEEPTTL`
`SET key val NX EX 30` is the canonical single-command atomic lock acquire — replaces the deprecated `SETNX` + `EXPIRE` pair which could leak a lock if the client died between commands
`SETEX key seconds value` and `PSETEX` are legacy sugar for the same thing; modern code should use `SET ... EX`
`MSET k1 v1 k2 v2` / `MGET k1 k2 k3` batch multiple keys in one round trip — one RTT instead of N, the single biggest latency win in most apps
`INCR`/`DECR`/`INCRBY`/`DECRBY` treat the string as a 64-bit signed integer, are atomic, and error with `value is not an integer or out of range` on non-numeric content
`INCRBYFLOAT` uses a long double; note it has no `DECRBYFLOAT` — pass a negative increment
Atomic counters are the reason `INCR` exists: read-modify-write in the app has a race, `INCR` does not; use for page views, rate limits, ID generation
`APPEND key value` is amortized O(1) and returns the new length — useful for accumulating log lines into a single key
Substring access: `GETRANGE key start end` (negative indices count from the end) and `SETRANGE key offset value` (zero-pads if it extends past the end)
`STRLEN key` is O(1); `GETDEL key` (atomic get-and-delete) and `GETEX key EX 60` (get and reset TTL) replace multi-command patterns
Encodings: `int` for integers up to 64 bits (shared objects 0–9999 cost nothing), `embstr` for strings ≤ 44 bytes (single allocation, cache-friendly), `raw` above that
Gotcha: repeated `APPEND` or `SETRANGE` flips an `embstr` to `raw` permanently and over-allocates capacity — a string that grew is fatter than one written at full size
Classic uses: cache a rendered fragment, store a session blob, hold a feature flag, count anything, implement a distributed lock

chapters.title: Bits and Bytes: Strings as Compact Structures
points: Bitmaps are not a separate type — they are ordinary strings addressed one bit at a time, so all string commands and TTLs still apply
`SETBIT key offset 0|1` sets a bit and returns the old bit; the string auto-grows and zero-fills, so `SETBIT k 10000000 1` immediately allocates ~1.2 MB
`GETBIT key offset` is O(1); offsets past the end read as 0
`BITCOUNT key [start end [BYTE|BIT]]` counts set bits — the daily-active-users primitive: one bit per user ID per day
Daily actives pattern: key `active:2026-09-07`, `SETBIT active:2026-09-07 <userId> 1` on login, `BITCOUNT` for the total — 1 million users costs 125 KB
`BITOP AND|OR|XOR|NOT dest src [src ...]` combines bitmaps — `BITOP AND weekly d1 d2 ... d7` gives users active every day of the week
`BITPOS key bit [start] [end]` finds the first 0 or 1 bit — used for free-slot allocation
`BITFIELD` packs multiple small integer counters into one string with `GET`/`SET`/`INCRBY` on arbitrary-width fields (`u4`, `i8`, …) and overflow policies `WRAP|SAT|FAIL`
Bitmap trade-off: dense IDs are extremely cheap, sparse IDs are wasteful — a bitmap sized by max ID, not by member count
HyperLogLog is also string-backed: `PFADD key element ...`, `PFCOUNT key [key ...]`, `PFMERGE dest src ...`
HLL gives approximate cardinality with 0.81% standard error in a fixed 12 KB, no matter whether you add a thousand or a billion items
Choose HLL over a set when you only need 'how many unique?' and never need to list or test members — `SCARD` is exact but stores every element
Comparison row — unique visitors: SET = exact + O(N) memory; bitmap = exact + needs integer IDs; HLL = approximate + constant 12 KB
Gotcha: `PFCOUNT` on a single key is O(1) but does mutate the key (caches the estimate), so it is technically a write command and fails on a read-only replica

chapters.title: Lists: Ordered Sequences and the Deque
points: A Redis list is an ordered sequence of strings, allowing duplicates, implemented as a quicklist — a linked list of ziplist/listpack nodes
Push and pop at both ends are O(1): `LPUSH`/`RPUSH` add, `LPOP`/`RPOP` remove; each push command accepts multiple values
`LPUSHX`/`RPUSHX` only push if the key already exists — prevents resurrecting a list that was intentionally trimmed away
`LLEN key` is O(1); `LRANGE key start stop` is O(S+N) where S is the offset — `LRANGE key 0 -1` on a huge list is a server-blocking mistake
Index access `LINDEX key i` is O(N) — a list is not an array; if you index by position frequently, you chose the wrong type
`LSET key index value` overwrites in place and errors with `index out of range` past the end; `LINSERT key BEFORE|AFTER pivot value` is O(N)
`LREM key count value` removes matching elements: positive count scans head→tail, negative tail→head, zero removes all
`LTRIM key start stop` keeps only a range and discards the rest — the capped-list idiom is `LPUSH` then `LTRIM key 0 999` to keep the latest 1000
Queue idiom: producers `LPUSH`, consumers `BRPOP key timeout` — blocking pop parks the client until an element arrives, with 0 meaning wait forever
Reliable queue idiom: `LMOVE src dst RIGHT LEFT` (and blocking `BLMOVE`) atomically moves the job to a processing list so a crashed worker does not lose it; `RPOPLPUSH` is the deprecated older name
`LMPOP numkeys key [key ...] LEFT|RIGHT [COUNT n]` pops from the first non-empty of several lists in one call; `BLMPOP` blocks
`LPOS key element [RANK r] [COUNT n]` finds the index of a matching element without pulling the whole list to the client
Encoding: small lists are a single `listpack` (contiguous, cache-friendly); past `list-max-listpack-size` they become a `quicklist` of linked nodes
Trade-off vs sorted set for a timeline: list gives O(1) prepend but no ranking or dedup; sorted set gives ordered range queries at O(log N) insert
Common mistake: using a list as a job queue with no cap or no `BLMOVE` — unbounded growth on producer spikes, silent job loss on worker crash

chapters.title: Sets: Membership and Set Algebra
points: A set is an unordered collection of unique strings — adding an existing member is a no-op that returns 0
`SADD key m [m ...]` and `SREM key m [m ...]` are O(N) in the number of members supplied, i.e. O(1) per member
`SISMEMBER key member` is O(1) — the fastest 'is X in the group?' check in Redis; `SMISMEMBER key m1 m2 ...` batches it
`SCARD key` returns cardinality in O(1); `SMEMBERS key` is O(N) and returns everything — dangerous on large sets, use `SSCAN` instead
`SPOP key [count]` removes and returns random members (a write); `SRANDMEMBER key [count]` returns without removing (a read)
`SRANDMEMBER` with a negative count may return the same member more than once and can return more elements than the set holds — positive count never repeats
`SINTER`/`SUNION`/`SDIFF` compute intersection, union, difference; the `*STORE` variants write the result into a destination key instead of shipping it to the client
`SINTERCARD numkeys k1 k2 [LIMIT n]` returns just the size of the intersection with an early-exit limit — avoids materializing a huge result
Complexity: `SINTER` is O(N*M) worst case (N = smallest set size, M = number of sets); Redis optimizes by starting from the smallest set
`SMOVE src dst member` atomically moves a member between sets — state-machine transitions without a race
Encodings: `intset` (sorted array of integers, tiny and cache-friendly) when all members are integers and count is small, `listpack` for small non-integer sets, `hashtable` above the thresholds
Encoding gotcha: adding one non-integer member to a large `intset` converts the whole thing to a `hashtable` and memory jumps sharply
Uses: tag systems, unique visitor IDs, follower/following lists, permission bundles, and 'people you both follow' via `SINTER`
Comparison row — set vs list: set gives O(1) membership and dedup but no order; list keeps order and duplicates but membership is O(N)
Common mistake: `SMEMBERS` on a set of hundreds of thousands of members inside a request path — it blocks the server and floods the network

chapters.title: Sorted Sets: Ranking, Ranges, and Leaderboards
points: A sorted set is a set of unique members, each with a float64 score; members are kept ordered by score, ties broken lexicographically by member
Implemented as a skip list plus a hash table: the skip list gives O(log N) ordered operations, the hash gives O(1) score lookup by member

`ZADD key score member [score member ...]` is O(log N) per member; flags `NX`/`XX` (add-only / update-only), `GT`/`LT` (only raise / only lower a score), `CH` (return changed count), `INCR` (behave like `ZINCRBY`)
`ZINCRBY key delta member` atomically bumps a score — the leaderboard update primitive; a missing member is treated as score 0
`ZSCORE key member` is O(1); `ZMSCORE` batches; `ZCARD` is O(1); `ZCOUNT key min max` is O(log N)
`ZRANK`/`ZREVRANK key member [WITHSCORE]` return the 0-based position in O(log N) — 'what place am I in?' without scanning
`ZRANGE key start stop [REV] [BYSCORE|BYLEX] [LIMIT offset count] [WITHSCORES]` is the modern unified range command; it subsumes the deprecated `ZREVRANGE`, `ZRANGEBYSCORE`, `ZRANGEBYLEX`
Score ranges use `-inf`/`+inf` and a `(` prefix for exclusive bounds: `ZRANGE key (100 200 BYSCORE`
`BYLEX` ranges (`[a`, `(a`, `-`, `+`) only give meaningful order when every member shares the same score — the autocomplete-prefix trick
Removal by position or value range: `ZREMRANGEBYRANK` (trim a leaderboard to top N), `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE` (expire old entries), `ZREMRANGEBYLEX`
`ZPOPMIN`/`ZPOPMAX` and blocking `BZPOPMIN`/`BZPOPMAX` turn a sorted set into a priority queue; `ZMPOP`/`BZMPOP` pop across multiple keys
`ZUNIONSTORE`/`ZINTERSTORE`/`ZDIFFSTORE` combine sorted sets with per-key `WEIGHTS` and `AGGREGATE SUM|MIN|MAX` — weighted scoring across signals in one command
Delayed-job / time-series idiom: score = unix timestamp, `ZRANGEBYSCORE key -inf <now> LIMIT 0 10` to fetch what is due, then `ZREM` it
Encoding: `listpack` for small sorted sets (linear scan, cheap), `skiplist` past `zset-max-listpack-entries`/`-value`
Trade-off: leaderboard on a sorted set is O(log N) writes and O(log N + M) page reads, versus sorting in the app which is O(N log N) plus shipping every row

chapters.title: Hashes: Field-Level Objects
points: A hash maps string fields to string values inside one key — the natural fit for an object with independently-updated attributes
`HSET key f v [f v ...]` sets one or many fields (`HMSET` is deprecated in favour of variadic `HSET`); `HSETNX` only writes a field that does not exist
`HGET key field` is O(1); `HMGET key f1 f2` fetches a subset; `HGETALL key` is O(N) over all fields and returns field/value pairs
`HDEL key f [f ...]`, `HEXISTS key field`, `HLEN key`, `HSTRLEN key field` round out the basics — all O(1) per field
`HINCRBY`/`HINCRBYFLOAT` give atomic per-field counters — a whole stats object in one key without read-modify-write races
`HKEYS`/`HVALS`/`HGETALL` are all O(N); on a hash with thousands of fields, iterate with `HSCAN key cursor [MATCH pat] [COUNT n]` instead
`HRANDFIELD key [count] [WITHVALUES]` samples fields; negative count allows repeats, mirroring `SRANDMEMBER`
Modern Redis supports per-field TTL: `HEXPIRE`/`HPEXPIRE`/`HEXPIREAT`, `HTTL`, `HPERSIST` — expire one field without touching the rest of the object
Hash vs serialized JSON string: hash lets you `HGET` one field and `HINCRBY` atomically; a JSON string forces read-parse-modify-write and a full-value transfer
JSON-in-a-string wins when you always read the whole object and want one round trip; hash wins when fields are updated independently or read selectively
Encoding: `listpack` (a flat array scanned linearly) while under `hash-max-listpack-entries` (128) and `hash-max-listpack-value` (64 bytes), `hashtable` above either threshold
Memory trick: sharding a million keys into hashes of ~100 fields each (`bucket:<id/100>` → field `<id%100>`) can cut memory several-fold, because listpack hashes avoid per-key overhead
Every top-level key carries overhead (robj, dict entry, expire entry, key string) — roughly 50–90 bytes before your data; hashes amortize that across fields
Limitation: hash fields cannot be nested and, aside from field TTLs, have no independent type — values are always strings
Common mistake: `HGETALL` on a hash used as a bucket of 100k fields — one command that transfers megabytes and stalls the event loop

chapters.title: Choosing the Right Type: Comparisons and Complexity
points: Decision question 1 — do I need uniqueness? Yes → set or sorted set. No → list or string
Decision question 2 — do I need order? Insertion order → list. Score order → sorted set. None → set or hash
Decision question 3 — do I address parts independently? Yes → hash. No → string
Comparison row — string: O(1) get/set, whole-value only, best for cache blobs, counters, flags, locks
Comparison row — list: O(1) ends, O(N) middle, duplicates allowed, best for queues, capped feeds, stacks
Comparison row — set: O(1) membership and add, unordered, unique, best for tags, relations, set algebra
Comparison row — sorted set: O(log N) add and rank, ordered by score, unique, best for leaderboards, priority queues, time-indexed data
Comparison row — hash: O(1) per field, unordered fields, best for objects and per-key stat groups
Watch list of O(N) commands that block the server: `KEYS`, `SMEMBERS`, `HGETALL`, `LRANGE 0 -1`, `ZRANGE 0 -1`, `SORT`, `DEL` on a huge collection, `FLUSHALL` without `ASYNC`
Rule of thumb: any command whose result size grows with the collection needs either a `LIMIT`/`COUNT` bound or a `*SCAN` cursor
Big-O is per command, but latency is per server: an O(N) command with N = 10^6 costs milliseconds of blocking for every other client, so 'fast' means 'bounded N'
Memory ordering, roughly small to large for the same data: intset < listpack < hashtable/skiplist; small collections are dramatically cheaper per element
Same data, three shapes: 1M user flags = 1M string keys (~80 MB overhead) vs 10k hashes of 100 fields (~a few MB) vs one bitmap (125 KB) — pick by what you must query
Counter-example to over-optimizing: the compact encodings are linear-scan, so a listpack hash with 500 fields is slower per lookup than a hashtable — thresholds exist for a reason

Types you graduate to when these run out: streams for append-only logs with consumer groups, geospatial (sorted-set-backed) for radius queries, JSON/Search modules for nested documents and secondary indexes

chapters.title: Working Patterns: Atomicity, Pipelines, and Expiry
points: Pipelining sends N commands without waiting for each reply — it collapses N round trips into one and is the single biggest throughput lever; it is not atomic

`MULTI` / command queue / `EXEC` is a transaction: commands are queued and executed serially with nothing interleaved, but there is no rollback — a runtime error in one command does not undo the others
`WATCH key` before `MULTI` gives optimistic locking: if the watched key changed, `EXEC` returns nil and the client retries — the check-and-set pattern
Lua scripts (`EVAL script numkeys key ... arg ...`, `EVALSHA`, `SCRIPT LOAD`) run atomically on the server: use them for read-then-write logic that must not interleave
Redis Functions (`FUNCTION LOAD`, `FCALL`) are the modern, persisted replacement for ad-hoc `EVAL` scripts
Keep scripts short — a slow Lua script blocks the whole server exactly like a slow command
Distributed lock, acquire: `SET lock:<res> <random-token> NX EX 30`; release must be a Lua script that deletes only if the value still matches the token, or you will delete someone else's lock
Expiry mechanics: keys are removed lazily on access plus by an active sampling cycle, so an expired key can occupy memory for a while after its TTL passes
Only top-level keys expire (except hash-field TTLs): you cannot expire a single list element or set member — model that with a sorted set scored by timestamp plus `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE`
Rate limiting, fixed window: `INCR ratelimit:<user>:<minute>` then `EXPIRE ... 60 NX` on first hit — cheap, but allows a 2x burst at the window boundary
Rate limiting, sliding window: sorted set of request timestamps, `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE key -inf <now-window>` then `ZCARD` then `ZADD` — accurate, more memory per user
Cache-aside pattern: `GET`, on miss load from the database, `SET key value EX ttl`; add a small random jitter to the TTL so a thundering herd does not all expire at once
Keyspace notifications (`notify-keyspace-events`) let you subscribe to expirations and evictions — useful for cleanup, but delivery is fire-and-forget, not a queue

`maxmemory` plus an eviction policy (`noeviction`, `allkeys-lru`, `volatile-ttl`, `allkeys-lfu`, …) decides what happens when memory fills — `noeviction` returns `OOM command not allowed` on writes instead of silently dropping data
`SCAN` and its type-specific siblings `SSCAN`/`HSCAN`/`ZSCAN` are the only safe way to walk a large keyspace or collection in production

chapters.title: Pitfalls, Diagnostics, and the Big Picture
points: Mistake — big keys: a single collection with millions of elements makes every touch slow, blocks failover, and cannot be sharded; find them with `redis-cli --bigkeys` or `MEMORY USAGE key`
Mistake — `KEYS *` in application code: O(N) over the whole keyspace with a single-threaded server; it is the most common cause of a production stall
Mistake — unbounded growth: a list, set, or sorted set with no `LTRIM`, `ZREMRANGEBYRANK`, or TTL will grow until eviction or OOM
Mistake — no TTL on cache keys: they never leave, and with `noeviction` writes start failing once `maxmemory` is reached
Mistake — wrong type for the access pattern: `LINDEX` in a loop, `SMEMBERS` then filtering client-side, JSON string re-written for a single field change
Mistake — N+1 round trips: N sequential `GET`s cost N network RTTs; replace with `MGET`, a pipeline, or a Lua script
Mistake — treating Redis as durable by default: `RDB` snapshots lose the window since the last save and `AOF` with `everysec` can lose ~1 second; choose the persistence mode deliberately
Cluster gotcha: multi-key commands (`SINTER`, `MGET`, `ZUNIONSTORE`) require all keys in the same hash slot — force it with a hash tag `{user1000}:profile`
Diagnostics — `SLOWLOG GET` lists commands that exceeded `slowlog-log-slower-than`; it is the first place to look when latency spikes
Diagnostics — `INFO memory` (`used_memory`, fragmentation ratio), `INFO stats` (`keyspace_hits`/`keyspace_misses` for hit rate), `INFO clients` (`blocked_clients`)
Diagnostics — `MONITOR` streams every command live; it is a debugging tool only, since it measurably slows the server
Diagnostics — `OBJECT ENCODING key` to confirm a collection is still in its compact encoding, and `redis-cli --latency` / `--memkeys` for latency and memory profiles
Sizing check before shipping: how many keys, how big is the biggest collection, what is the TTL, what happens at 10x — answer all four or you are guessing
Summary of the mental model: pick the type by access pattern, keep every N bounded, batch your round trips, and give every key a lifecycle
One-line recap per type — string: a byte array with a counter bolted on; list: a deque; set: membership and algebra; sorted set: an index you can rank; hash: an object with addressable fields
